content: 1. Ciprofloxacin has been studied in pediatric populations globally under compassionate use programs, with safety data reported in the Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal in 1997. Additionally, the rheumatologic effects of fluoroquinolone treatment in pediatric cystic fibrosis patients were explored in the same journal. 2. 3. The FDA has reinforced safety warnings regarding serious side effects of fluoroquinolone antibiotics, including hypoglycemia and mental health disturbances, necessitating label changes. Furthermore, disabling and potentially permanent side effects have led to restrictions on the use of these antibiotics. 4. Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are now recommended only when other commonly prescribed antibiotics are deemed inappropriate, as per updated safety guidelines. 5. Studies have evaluated the outcomes of young children exposed to multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) over a 30-month follow-up period, as well as the treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in contacts of MDR-TB patients using alternative regimens like linezolid monotherapy. 6. The WHO has issued consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT), emphasizing the identification of at-risk populations, screening for active TB, testing for TB infection, and selecting appropriate TPT regimens. These guidelines aim to enhance global implementation and contribute to ending the TB epidemic. 7. Recommendations include offering TPT to individuals living with HIV, household contacts of TB patients, and other high-risk groups. Specific regimens include 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid, 3 months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or 4 months of daily rifampicin. Alternative regimens, such as 1 month of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid, are also conditionally recommended. 8. For contacts exposed to MDR-TB, 6 months of daily levofloxacin is recommended as a preventive treatment option. 9. The guidelines also address the use of diagnostic tools, such as chest X-rays, molecular tests, and C-reactive protein levels, to screen for TB disease in various populations, including those living with HIV. 10. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of systematic screening and testing for TB infection in high-risk groups, including prisoners, healthcare workers, migrants from high TB burden countries, and individuals preparing for organ transplants or receiving dialysis. 11. The development of these guidelines involved a rigorous process, including evidence reviews, expert panel discussions, and the use of the GRADE methodology to assess the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. 12. The updated guidelines incorporate findings from recent clinical trials and align with revised WHO recommendations on TB screening and diagnostics. They also provide practical details on dosing schedules, adherence support, and minimizing treatment toxicity. 13. The aim of these guidelines is to support effective scaling up of TPT globally, enabling tailored management approaches for different target groups and contexts, and providing a foundation for updating national TPT guidelines. 14. The guidelines were developed with input from a diverse group of experts, including national TB program managers, researchers, and patient representatives, ensuring a comprehensive and inclusive approach. 15. The recommendations are based on high-certainty evidence from randomized controlled trials and other studies, with a focus on balancing the benefits and risks of TPT regimens. 16. The WHO guidelines also address the operational aspects of TPT implementation, including monitoring, evaluation, and addressing research gaps to improve programmatic management. These interpretations reflect the detailed content of the guidelines and associated studies, providing a clear and professional summary of the key points.
